extracted.intended_audience: USPTO-registered patent practitioners, disciplinary counsel, and attorneys facing USPTO disciplinary proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria used by the USPTO (and ALJ) to evaluate alleged violations of the Rules of Professional Conduct by practitioners, and to determine appropriate sanctions (suspension/exclusion). Applies to conduct before the USPTO under 37 C.F.R. part 11 and related statutes/case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority and grounds for discipline (35 U.S.C. § 32 / 37 C.F.R. § 11.19)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director of the USPTO may suspend or exclude a person from practice before the Office if the person is 'shown to be incompetent or disreputable, or guilty of gross misconduct,' or if the person violates regulations established by the Office (35 U.S.C. § 32; 37 C.F.R. § 11.19(b)(1)(iv)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited authorities (e.g., Kroll v. Finnerty, Sperry) confirm USPTO's exclusive authority to regulate practice before it. This is the statutory/fundamental basis for imposing discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof (37 C.F.R. § 11.49)
rubrics_metrics.description: The OED Director has the burden of proving the alleged violations by clear and convincing evidence; thereafter Respondent bears the burden to prove any affirmative defense by clear and convincing evidence (37 C.F.R. § 11.49).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision explains the clear-and-convincing standard using case law: intermediate between preponderance and beyond a reasonable doubt (Addington), requires evidence producing 'a firm belief or conviction' (Jimenez), and evidence that is 'certain, unambiguous, and plain' (Foster). This standard governs factual findings and is applied to protect important liberty interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct apply (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.101-11.901)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective May 3, 2013, the USPTO promulgated Rules of Professional Conduct (modeled on ABA standards) which govern conduct of persons authorized to practice before the Office; accused practitioners must receive notice and opportunity for a hearing (35 U.S.C. § 32).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules supply the substantive ethics/regulatory requirements (communication, fee division, competence, conduct prejudicial to administration of justice, etc.) referenced throughout disciplinary evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'practice before the Office' (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Practice before the Office' includes any law-related service connected with presentation to the Office relating to a client's rights, privileges, duties, or responsibilities under laws or regulations administered by the Office, including preparing documents in contemplation of filing and communicating with and advising a client concerning matters pending or contemplated to be presented before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.5(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples treated as 'practice' include drafting responses to Office actions, counseling clients on prosecution strategy, advising about legal significance of Office correspondence, and strategizing about filings. Whether someone is 'practicing' is fact-specific and central to unauthorized-practice claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on assisting unauthorized practice (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall not practice law in a jurisdiction in violation of that jurisdiction's regulations, or assist another in doing so; the USPTO is a jurisdiction for this purpose (37 C.F.R. § 11.505).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prove assistance, the Office must show (1) the other person engaged in unauthorized practice before the Office, and (2) the practitioner facilitated or enabled that practice (citing prior USPTO disciplinary precedent). Conduct that lends a suspended practitioner's authority (e.g., use of another's registration number to cover activity) can constitute assisting unauthorized practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules governing suspended/excluded practitioners (37 C.F.R. § 11.58)
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended or excluded practitioner must, within 30 days, file a notice of withdrawal in each matter pending before the Office, notify clients of the order and inability to act, and either conclude the work or advise the client to make other arrangements. A suspended/excluded practitioner may only act as a paralegal or assistant under a practitioner's direct supervision as a salaried employee and is barred from communicating directly with clients or rendering legal advice in matters before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(b),(c),(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to withdraw or to notify clients, or allowing an excluded practitioner to continue counseling clients or holding out as authorized, constitutes unauthorized practice and regulatory violations. Practitioners who employ or work with suspended attorneys must ensure compliance with these strict limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fee division requirements (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b) and (e))
rubrics_metrics.description: Dividing fees with attorneys not in the same firm or otherwise must comply with the Rules; in particular, fee-splitting requires disclosure and client consent (37 C.F.R. § 11.105(b),(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision treats undisclosed fee divisions and absence of client consent as violations. Evidence about who collected fees, who was paid, and whether clients were informed is central to proving impermissible fee division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duties of communication to clients (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.102(a), 11.104(a)(2), 11.104(a)(3), 11.104(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must reasonably consult with clients about objectives and how to accomplish them (11.102(a)); keep clients reasonably informed of the status of matters (11.104(a)(3)); explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to permit clients to make informed decisions (11.104(a)(2)); and disclose basis of fees and fee division where applicable (11.104(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures cited include not informing clients of suspension of co-counsel, not notifying clients of Notices of Abandonment, and not providing contact information. The decision treats such failures as breaches of client duties even where communications occurred indirectly via another attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on dishonesty, deceit, misrepresentation, and conduct prejudicial to administration of justice (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(c) & (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 11.804(c) proscribes conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit, or misrepresentation; § 11.804(d) proscribes conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. Such conduct undermines public confidence and is sanctionable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: allowing a suspended attorney to conceal suspension by using another practitioner's registration number or otherwise hiding disciplinary status constitutes deceit and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice. Prejudice includes harm to public perception and self-regulation of the bar, even absent concrete client injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility and oversight of the registered attorney (gatekeeping duty)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registered practitioner who serves as the attorney of record has the ultimate responsibility to ensure representations comply with the Rules of Professional Conduct, including oversight of communications, fee disclosures, and ensuring that any persons assisting (including formerly-registered attorneys) comply with § 11.58 limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing under one's registration number while allowing another (suspended) person to counsel clients or set fees without oversight can constitute failure to discharge duties and facilitate unauthorized practice. Registered practitioners must exercise supervision and not rely solely on a co-attorney's representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctioning framework and factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b) and ABA Standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before imposing sanctions the Court considers: (1) whether the practitioner violated a duty to a client/public/legal system/profession; (2) whether the practitioner acted intentionally, knowingly, or negligently; (3) the amount of actual or potential injury; and (4) existence of aggravating or mitigating factors (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)). The Court often looks to the ABA STANDARDS FOR IMPOSING LAWYER SANCTIONS for guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggravating factors discussed include dishonest/selfish motive, failure to acknowledge wrongful nature, and substantial experience; mitigating factors include absence of prior discipline. The presence or absence of actual client injury, the intent/knowledge of the practitioner, and experience level weigh heavily in determining severity (e.g., length of suspension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental state / culpability (intentional, knowing, negligent)
rubrics_metrics.description: The practitioner's state of mind (intentional, knowing, or negligent conduct) is a core factor in sanction assessment and in characterizing the seriousness of the violation (37 C.F.R. § 11.54(b)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge that a co-practitioner was suspended and nonetheless facilitating their continued representation supports finding knowing or intentional assistance in unauthorized practice, increasing sanction severity; negligent lapses in client communication are treated less severely but still relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actual vs. potential injury to clients or the justice system
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of actual or potential injury caused by the practitioner's misconduct informs sanction severity; lack of evidence of actual client injury can mitigate severity even where potential for harm existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision weighs absence of documented client harm as a mitigating consideration, while noting that assisting unauthorized practice is 'intrinsically detrimental' to administration of justice and thus always carries potential systemic injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes permissible assistance by suspended/excluded attorneys
rubrics_metrics.description: A suspended/excluded practitioner may assist another practitioner only as a paralegal or assistant under direct supervision and as a salaried employee, and must not provide legal advice or communicate directly with clients about matters before the Office (37 C.F.R. § 11.58(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes permissible relationships (e.g., draftsman, foreign counsel where not suspended) from impermissible circumvention (where the suspended person continues to counsel, set fees, or communicate with clients). The arrangement must meet the specific §11.58 requirements to be lawful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of precedent and case law to define violations and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO disciplinary decisions rely on prior USPTO precedents and federal/state case law (e.g., Kroll v. Finnerty, Sperry, In re Piccone) to interpret 'practice before the Office', 'assistance', and ethical duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of conduct references analogous decisions and precedent to determine whether specific acts (e.g., being listed as attorney-of-record, drafting responses, counseling clients) amount to practice before the Office or violations of specific Rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanction outcome considerations and proportionality
rubrics_metrics.description: The ALJ must balance all factors — violation(s), culpability, injury, aggravating/mitigating circumstances — to craft a proportional sanction (suspension length, conditions for reinstatement). The decision cites application of those factors resulting in a two-year suspension in this case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when violations are knowing and serious, absence of prior discipline and lack of demonstrable client harm may reduce recommended suspension from the maximum sought by OED. The decision demonstrates application of the framework to justify less-than-requested sanction.
